passage: The monthly review at the cooperative bank in Sangli had gone well, Anand thought: Disha's loan files were the neatest in the branch, and farmers asked for her by name. So he was surprised to find her at her counter afterwards, blinking hard, stamping forms too firmly. 'Everything all right?' 'You said I'm slow at the counter,' she said. 'In front of everyone.' He took the review sheet from his folder and pulled a chair up beside her. 'Let me read it out. All of it.' He read slowly: neat files, zero errors in three months, patient with elderly customers, trusted by farmers. 'Counter speed at rush hour could improve.' He looked up. 'What else does this page say?' Disha looked at it a long moment. 'That I'm doing the job well,' she said. 'Mostly.' 'Not mostly. Well. With one thing to practise.'

qa.q: How many errors had Disha made in three months?
qa.a: Disha had zero errors in three months.

qa.q: Why is Disha stamping forms too firmly after the review?
qa.a: Disha is hurt and embarrassed, because the one line about counter speed, said in front of everyone, has become the whole review in her mind.

qa.q: Why was Anand's question 'What else does this page say?' useful?
qa.a: It let Disha find the good parts herself instead of being told to cheer up, while keeping counter speed as one real thing to practise.

qa.q: What might Anand learn from Disha's reaction?
qa.a: Anand may realise that one line said in front of others can drown out a lot of praise, and might read the whole sheet privately in future reviews.

grounding: Shows a branch manager who sees a clerk leave a good review sure she was criticised, and reads the whole sheet aloud and asks what else it says.

passage: After the quarterly review in the small Prague office, Camila went straight to the kitchen and stood staring at the kettle without switching it on. Jana, her team lead, found her there. 'You look like someone who got bad news.' 'You said my presentations run long,' Camila said. 'That's what everyone will remember.' Jana went back to her desk, printed the review and brought it to the kitchen. 'I'm going to read it out loud. Stop me when you hear something bad.' She read: best client feedback on the team, the Vienna account saved, two interns mentored, and one line, 'presentations could be tighter'. Camila didn't stop her once until the end. 'So what else does it say?' Jana asked. Camila finally switched on the kettle. 'That the Vienna account was mine.'

qa.q: Which account did Camila save?
qa.a: Camila saved the Vienna account.

qa.q: What does Camila staring at the kettle without switching it on suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Camila is lost in the one line about long presentations, so upset that the rest of the review has faded out.

qa.q: What made Jana's way of reading the review effective?
qa.a: Reading it aloud and asking Camila to stop at anything bad showed that only one line was critical, and asking 'what else does it say?' let Camila name the good news herself.

qa.q: If Jana had simply said 'Don't worry about it', what might have changed?
qa.a: Camila might have kept worrying, because the rest of the page would still be unheard, and the Vienna success would stay buried under one line.

passage:
The quarterly review at the city museum's education department had gone well, Dilnaz thought. Maria's school tours were the most booked in the building.

So she was surprised, an hour later, to find Maria in the storeroom, sorting worksheets that didn't need sorting, jaw tight.

"All okay?"

"You said I need to delegate more," Maria said. "In front of everyone. So I'm basically not good enough to lead."

Dilnaz went back to her desk, printed the review, and came back. "Can I read you the whole page?"

She read it aloud, slowly. "Tours booked out every week. Teachers ask for you by name. Your new worksheet for Class 5 is now used across the department. You trained two volunteers. One area to grow: delegate more so you don't burn out."

She handed the page over. "What else does it say?"

Maria read it again, silently. Her shoulders came down a little. "It says I'm doing well," she said. "And one thing to work on."

qa.q: What did Maria's new worksheet become, according to the review?
qa.a: It is now used across the department.

qa.q: Why was Maria so sure she had been criticised?
qa.a: The one line about delegating stung, especially in front of others, so it blocked out the rest of the review. Her mind turned a small tip into "not good enough to lead".

qa.q: What worked about Dilnaz reading the whole page aloud and asking "What else does it say?"
qa.a: It brought all the praise back into view without arguing with Maria, and the question let Maria find the balance herself. She ended by naming both the praise and the one thing to work on.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz have felt finding Maria in the storeroom after a review she thought went well?
qa.a: Dilnaz was probably surprised and concerned, since the review was meant to be positive. It showed her how one line can land harder than intended.

grounding: A team lead sees an employee leave a good review convinced she was criticised because of one line, and reads the whole page aloud to help her see the rest.

Subject: About this morning's review

Hi Zeenat,

I noticed you went very quiet after our review meeting, and at lunch you told Priya that "Tanuja thinks my reports are sloppy." I don't want you to spend the weekend on that, so here's the full page, word for word:

"Zeenat's client reports are thorough and well researched. Clients have renewed three contracts, partly because of her follow-up calls. She mentored the new intern without being asked. Her data is always accurate. Suggestion: the formatting could be more consistent across reports."

That's it. One line about formatting. Everything else is praise, and I meant all of it.

When you read the whole thing, what else does it say to you?

If you'd like, we can sit for ten minutes on Monday and I can share the template I use for formatting. It took me years to stop fussing over mine.

Warmly,
Tanuja

qa.q: How many contracts have clients renewed, partly because of Zeenat's follow-up calls?
qa.a: Clients have renewed three contracts.

qa.q: What does Zeenat telling Priya "Tanuja thinks my reports are sloppy" suggest about how she heard the review?
qa.a: It suggests Zeenat felt hurt and judged, having filtered out all the praise so that the one formatting line felt like the whole message.

qa.q: Why is asking "what else does it say to you?" better than just saying "You're doing great"?
qa.a: It invites Zeenat to reread the page and notice the praise herself instead of only being reassured. Finding it herself is more likely to stick.

qa.q: What might Tanuja have been feeling when she heard what Zeenat told Priya at lunch?
qa.a: Tanuja was probably concerned that the praise had not come through, so she sent the full page and offered help before the weekend.

passage: People ask me, as a new team lead, what surprised me most. Here's one. I'm Mridul, I've had the job eight months, and last week I did a quarterly review with Rashmi, one of our best analysts. The written review was glowing: clear thinking, reliable, great with clients. One line said, 'Could delegate more.' She walked out of the room white-faced. An hour later she messaged asking if she was being put on a performance plan. My stomach dropped; clearly something had landed wrong. So I called her back in, put the page on the table and read the whole thing aloud, slowly, every line. Then I asked, 'What else does it say, apart from delegation?' She was quiet. Then she said, 'That I'm... good?' 'That you're very good,' I said. 'And that you could hand off a bit more.' She laughed, a little shaky.

qa.q: What did the one critical line in Rashmi's review say?
qa.a: It said, 'Could delegate more.'

qa.q: What did Mridul feel when Rashmi asked about a performance plan?
qa.a: Mridul felt a jolt of worry and some guilt, sensing that the review had been misread and something had gone wrong in how it landed.

qa.q: Why was reading the whole page aloud a good move?
qa.a: It made Rashmi hear every positive line, not only the one she had fixed on, and asking 'What else does it say?' let her find the balance herself.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi leave convinced she was in trouble?
qa.a: Rashmi's attention locked onto 'Could delegate more', and the fear it stirred filtered out all the praise, so a glowing review felt like criticism.

grounding: A team lead sees an employee leave a glowing review convinced she was criticised, then reads the whole page aloud and asks what else it says.

passage: I lead a small support team, and on Tuesday I did Pradeep's six-month review. By any measure it was good: fastest ticket times on the team, warm customer feedback, and one line suggesting he document his fixes more. He nodded through it, said thanks, and left. I didn't think much of it until lunch, when I saw him at his desk with the printout, a pen circle around that one line. He wasn't eating. Later he came over and asked, 'Disha, is documentation a firing thing here?' I can't say what was going on inside him, but it looked like one sentence had eaten the page. So at four I pulled a chair over and asked him to read the review to me, all of it. Then I asked, 'What else does it say?' He read it again, slower. 'That I'm fast,' he said. 'And that people like me.'

qa.a: He had circled the line suggesting he document his fixes more.

qa.q: What did Disha feel on seeing the circled line and the uneaten lunch?
qa.a: Disha grew concerned, sensing that one sentence had crowded out the rest of a good review, though Disha couldn't be sure what Pradeep was thinking.

qa.q: How did Disha help Pradeep see the full review?
qa.a: Disha asked Pradeep to read the whole review aloud and then asked what else it said, letting him find the praise himself.

qa.q: How did the review seem to feel to Pradeep before he reread it?
qa.a: It seemed to feel like a warning; the one line about documentation filtered out the praise, so he feared being fired.

passage:
Pranav, you asked what I learned as a young team lead. Let your old Tushar mama tell you about Rekha. When I was twenty-six, leading a small team at a textile mill in Surat, Rekha had her first annual review with me and the manager. It was a very good review. Nine lines of praise. One line: "Should share updates earlier."

She walked out pale. At lunch she told me, "They think I hide things. It was a terrible review."

I didn't argue. I fetched the review sheet and read the whole page aloud, slowly. "Excellent quality control." "Trusted by the floor workers." "Ready for more responsibility." Then I asked, "What else does it say, apart from updates?"

She sat quiet. "That I'm good at my job," she said. "I didn't hear any of that."

People hear the one line that hurts, Pranav. Sometimes you have to read them the rest.

qa.a: The line said, "Should share updates earlier."

qa.q: What did young Tushar feel seeing Rekha walk out pale?
qa.a: Young Tushar felt concerned, knowing the review was very good and sensing she had fixed on one line.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Rekha see the review?
qa.a: Tushar read the whole page aloud and asked what else it said, so Rekha heard the praise she had missed.

qa.q: How did Rekha experience the review at first?

He had written the review himself with the manager. It said: "Outstanding debugging. Mentors juniors. Delivered the billing module early. Should document code more consistently."

Francis turned the screen towards her and read aloud, line by line, slowly. When he reached "delivered the billing module early", Parveen let out a breath.

"I only saw the documentation line," she said.
"It's one line," Francis said. "The rest is you too."

In my first year as a team lead, I learned something from Harsha. After her quarterly review, she walked back to her desk with her jaw tight and didn't speak all afternoon. I was puzzled. I'd written that review. It was one of the best on the team.
Around five, I asked her for a coffee. She said, "I know I'm not doing well. You said my reports are late." I had written that. One line. Reports sometimes late.
So I took the printout and read it aloud, slowly, the whole page. Her work with the vendors. The new tracker she built. How the team relies on her. Then the late reports. I asked, "What else does this page say, apart from the reports?" She was quiet, then read a line back to me. "Team relies on her." Her shoulders came down a little.
I've read every review aloud since then.
— Darshan

qa.a: She built a new tracker.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel when Harsha came back from the review so tense?
qa.a: Darshan felt puzzled and concerned, since the review Darshan had written was one of the best on the team.

qa.q: What did Darshan do that helped Harsha see the full review?
qa.a: Darshan read the whole page aloud, then asked what else it said besides the reports, so Harsha found the good lines herself.

qa.q: How might Harsha have seen the review before it was read aloud?

passage:
Team lead's note, customer insights team, by Pallavi
Anjali's half-yearly review was strong. Our manager praised her analysis, her client presentation and her mentoring of interns. At the very end he said, "Maybe speak up more in team meetings." After the meeting, Anjali told me, "So basically I'm too quiet and nobody notices my work." I hadn't expected that.
I asked her to sit with me and I read the whole review sheet aloud. Six strengths, one suggestion. I stopped after each one. Then I asked, "What else does this say about you?" She read back, slowly, "Strong analysis. Best client deck this quarter." She looked surprised, as if she hadn't heard it the first time.
What I did next: I suggested she take one small speaking slot in Monday's team meeting, to work on the suggestion without forgetting everything else the review said.

qa.q: How many strengths were on Anjali's review sheet?
qa.a: Six strengths, and one suggestion.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when Anjali said nobody noticed her work?
qa.a: Pallavi felt surprised and concerned, since the review had actually been strong.

qa.q: Why was reading the sheet aloud and pausing a good approach?
qa.a: It gave each strength its own moment and let Anjali find the praise herself, while still leaving room to work on the one suggestion.

qa.q: How did the review look to Anjali before Pallavi read it aloud?
qa.a: Anjali had fixed on the last line and felt she was seen as too quiet and unnoticed.

grounding: A team lead's note shows an employee fixing on one line of a strong review, and the lead reading the whole sheet aloud and asking what else it says.

passage:
Wednesday night

Ramesh's half-year review today. Honestly one of the best I've written: he shipped the billing fix early, juniors go to him first, two clients ask for him by name. One line said his status updates could be shorter.
He walked out of the room looking like I'd fired him. At tea he said, "So I'm too slow with updates. Got it." Not a word about the rest.
I felt awful, like I'd written it badly. So I called him back in, put the page between us and read the whole thing aloud, every line, slowly. Then I asked, "What else does this page say?"
He was quiet for a long time. Then: "That... people rely on me?"
Tomorrow I'll send it again with the good parts first.

Usha

qa.q: Which line in the review did Ramesh fix on?
qa.a: The line saying his status updates could be shorter.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when Ramesh walked out of the room?
qa.a: Usha felt awful and a little guilty, worried the review had been written badly, because a mostly glowing review had landed as criticism.

qa.q: Why did reading the whole page aloud help?
qa.a: It made Ramesh hear every line, not only the painful one, and the open question let him find the praise himself instead of being told to cheer up.

qa.q: What was the review like for Ramesh before Usha read it aloud?
qa.a: For Ramesh it felt like a telling-off about slow updates; the praise about the billing fix, the juniors and the clients did not register at all.
